title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: CISA and FBI: a compromised ICS integrator held utilities’ SCADA data — limit what yours can reach
items.content_text: CISA and the FBI released a joint fact sheet on 24 September, “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators” (dated 23 September). Its motivating case: in March–April 2025, foreign actors inside a US industrial automation company that does system integration and SCADA programming for customers including power utilities and transportation entities searched for “customers” and “SCADA” and staged nine archives of about 800 files — customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics — for exfiltration. The agencies do not name the company, the actor or its country, and do not say any utility was breached. Their advice: write security and supply-chain requirements into integrator contracts, apply least privilege, route remote access through monitored, logged and preferably on-demand paths, know what data integrators hold and where, and be able to operate if an integrator is compromised.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA/FBI joint fact sheet, dated 23 Sep and released 24 Sep 2026 (primary), corroborated by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Published 24 Sep 2026; cites a March–April 2025 intrusion at the integrator

items.title: Three clusters are exploiting Cisco firewall-manager flaws CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316; one shares tooling with Sandworm
items.content_text: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079, a CVSS 10.0 flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker gain root on Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center, is being exploited; CISA added it to KEV that day with a 12 September deadline, now passed. Cisco Talos describes three clusters. UAT-12197 (unattributed) exploited CVE-2026-20079. UAT-11823 exploited both CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316 (CVSS 5.3, static credentials), deployed Cyclops Blink, a malware family previously attributed to Sandworm, and “overlaps in tooling with the Sandworm APT actor” — an overlap, not an attribution. UAT-11988, a ransomware operator, logged in using the CVE-2026-20316 static credentials, and its later actions were “consistent with those of Qilin ransomware affiliates.” Cisco shipped a hardening release on 16 September. Talos last updated its post on 21 September and names no victims or sectors; no new development was reported as of 27 September. FMC configures the firewalls that separate corporate networks from generation, substation and DER control.

items.title: Check Point management-server and VPN-gateway flaws were exploited before KEV listing; the federal deadline passed on 25 September
items.content_text: CISA added two Check Point flaws to KEV on 22 September. CVE-2026-93616 is a pre-authentication path traversal in Security Management Server, Multi-Domain Security Management, Log Server and SmartEvent that lets an attacker upload and run scripts; it was exploited as a zero-day on 23 July, and Check Point says a handful of customers were attacked. CVE-2026-85102 is an improper certificate-validation flaw that gives unauthenticated remote code execution on Security Gateway and Spark firewalls running site-to-site or remote-access VPN, with an exploitation wave from 12 September. For a utility these appliances often terminate the VPNs that contractors and integrators use to reach plant and substation networks. The same 22 September KEV batch added F5 BIG-IP APM CVE-2026-94127 (OAuth-profile configurations only) and Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator CVE-2026-93952; all four deadlines fell on 25 September. No power-sector victim has been named.

items.title: CenterPoint Energy confirms a breach of about 7.5 million customer records; the actor threatens to target “infrastructure” next
items.content_text: CenterPoint Energy, which serves roughly 7 million electric and gas customers across Texas, Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio, told the SEC on 15 September that an unauthorized third party had obtained customer personal information through one of its externally facing systems. A threat actor had posted a 2.5 GB archive it claimed held about 7.5 million records on a cybercrime forum on 12 September, adding: “next time we won’t simply pull data, we’ll start attacking the main infrastructure.” CenterPoint says the incident has not affected electric or gas delivery and, based on its investigation so far, does not expect a material impact; no vulnerability, intrusion vector or actor identity has been disclosed. This reads as an IT-side data breach, not an OT compromise — but the actor’s own words, and CenterPoint’s history of prior IT intrusions (an access broker in 2024, exposure via the Cl0p MOVEit campaign), are reason enough for other utilities to check that customer-facing systems are properly segmented from anything that touches control-system networks.
tags: Incident — Confirmed customer-data breach at a US electric & gas utility

items.title: Red Heron, assessed as PRC-linked, stole secrets and planted SSH keys in a renewable operator’s code server
items.content_text: Acronis reported on 13 September that an actor it tracks as Red Heron exploited CVE-2026-60004, a critical remote-code-execution flaw in self-hosted Gitea, to compromise 11 targets in five countries (Canada, the US, Taiwan, Argentina and Sri Lanka). The clearest power-sector case: a Canadian renewable-energy operator, where Acronis documented 22 exploitation sessions; the actor took source code, credentials and secrets, mapped internal Docker networks, and planted its own SSH keys for return access. Acronis holds the PRC-linked attribution at moderate confidence; nothing here shows hands-on manipulation of grid control, but the stolen credentials and network map are exactly what a follow-on intrusion would need. The campaign also exposed a previously undocumented Linux rootkit, SIXZUT. Gitea’s fix has been available since 27 July, and CISA’s KEV deadline passed a month ago; no new development was reported as of 27 September.

items.title: Forescout study of 47,700 network segments: only 13% of those holding OT devices are OT-only
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs published a 22 September analysis of 47,700 network segments containing more than 2.5 million devices across 209 organizations. Only 13% of segments containing OT devices were OT-only; the rest also held other types of device, and almost half mixed OT with both IT and IoT assets. Forescout also measured each sector’s average “blast radius” — devices per segment — at 9 for utilities, against 29 for manufacturing and 72 for oil and gas. Utilities fared better than most on that measure, but the core finding still applies: a mixed segment is what turns an IT-side credential theft, an exploited management console (see this edition’s Cisco and Check Point items) or a compromised integrator account into a path onto generation, substation or DER control networks, rather than a contained incident.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Forescout Vedere Labs, 22 Sep 2026 (primary), reported by Industrial Cyber 24 Sep 2026

items.title: Citrix confirms two NetScaler zero-days were exploited before a fix existed; both are now in CISA KEV with a 30 September deadline
items.content_text: Citrix confirmed on 27 September, a day after watchTowr’s disclosure, that CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (both CVSS 9.5) had been exploited against NetScaler ADC and Gateway before patches existed. CVE-2026-88771 is an improper-input-validation flaw giving unauthenticated remote code execution regardless of configuration; CVE-2026-88772 is a memory overflow reachable when DTLS is enabled, the default for VPN virtual servers. CISA added both to KEV the same day with a 30 September federal deadline. Citrix’s bulletin CTX697096 also fixes six other flaws (CVE-2026-88773 through -88778, CVSS 7.0–9.3) not reported as exploited. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.37 and 13.1-64.23 (and FIPS equivalents); no workaround exists. No actor has been named. NetScaler Gateway is a common remote-access front door into utility corporate networks and, from there, OT DMZs.

items.title: CISA adds a third exploited MikroTik RouterOS flaw to KEV; paired with an earlier one it gives password-free admin access
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-67279, an SSH workflow bypass in MikroTik RouterOS rated CVSS 6.9, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 25 September with a 28 September federal deadline. It joins CVE-2026-86060 and CVE-2026-67277, added on 10 September. CERT Polska reported in-the-wild exploitation from about 2 September of a two-flaw SSH chain it calls “MikroTrick”; its 22 September technical analysis names the chain as CVE-2026-67279 combined with CVE-2026-86060, which gives an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control. Fixed releases are RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21; the related CVE-2026-67278 needs 7.24.3 or 7.23.6. Shadowserver counted more than 122,500 MikroTik devices with SSH reachable from the internet in early September — an exposure count, not a count of compromised or unpatched devices. Editorial assessment: RouterOS is common on cellular and backhaul routers at small remote sites, which for a power operator can mean substations, solar and wind sites, and telemetry links.

items.title: A predictable session ID lets an attacker bypass authentication on Siemens’ Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay
items.content_text: Siemens disclosed CVE-2026-62645 on 8 September as part of that month’s ICS Patch Tuesday batch: a CVSS 9.8 missing-authentication flaw (CWE-306) in the Reyrolle 7SR5 protection relay’s web interface. The relay exposes information that lets an attacker calculate current and past session IDs, defeating the login entirely. All versions before V2.70 are affected. No in-the-wild exploitation or public exploit code has been reported. Protection relays like this trip breakers to protect equipment during faults; an attacker with unauthenticated access could, in principle, alter settings or block a legitimate trip, though doing so would require network reach to the relay first.

items.title: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s incident-reporting clock started running on 11 September
items.content_text: As of 11 September, manufacturers of connected products sold into the EU — a list that includes most of the vendors behind generation, substation and DER equipment — must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents to ENISA’s new Single Reporting Platform within set deadlines, even for products already installed and still within their support window. The rule applies to embedded software, control systems and networking gear, not just finished consumer devices. For a US utility this mostly shows up indirectly, in tighter and more standardized vendor disclosure timelines, but multinational vendors and integrators with EU operations should confirm their own reporting processes are live.
